name: an asymmetric dark grey-black crack: one long wandering diagonal stem with a single short side branch on one side and a tiny spur on the other, a short dirt-filled opening along the stem and lit lips under its flatter stretches, drawn as a transparent decal on old asphalt
label: wasteland_ruins/road-crack-b

surfaces.part: asphalt patch with crack decal, seen from above

answer.evidence: The object is a flat floor decal: a 48x48 grey asphalt patch with a thin dark crack and a few dirt patches, viewed straight from above. The column scan shows uniform grey rows (L~75-77) from row 3 to row 45, with only a brown dirt border at the edges. There is no front face, no front-edge line and no eave shadow, and the silhouette is a constant 48 px wide on every row. The dark rows near 44-46 are the border of the patch and do not form a vertical face. This is the intended look for a flat ground decal, so it reads as a top-down slab.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 8 visible tones per 16x16 tile, against 7 for the paving reference and 3 for the grass reference. Near-flat coverage is 0%, the same as both references, so no 5x5 area is a single flat colour. Only 6% of its dark edge pixels are neutral, so the crack edges and darks lean brown or tinted rather than black. This is unlike the paving reference, where 80% are neutral. The asphalt carries speckle and grain, and the crack has a dark core, a dirt-filled opening and lit lips under its flatter stretches. That gives roughly 5 lightness steps, close to the references. It uses only 11 colours in total, so the texture is less varied than a full Beodeul piece, but a locked palette explains that. Nothing reads as a sticker, and a careful artist would accept it next to the references.
